analysis.one_liner: Gives wheelchair users and independent shops the legal right to repair powered wheelchairs and mobility devices.
analysis.headline: The Wheelchair Right to Repair Act, introduced with one cosponsor, sits in two House committees with no action since it was referred in August 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Powered wheelchairs and scooters contain software locks and diagnostic tools that manufacturers restrict, so owners often must go through the manufacturer or an authorized dealer for repairs — which can mean weeks without a chair. The bill changes federal copyright law so it is legal to bypass those locks for repair, and requires manufacturers to sell owners and independent repair shops the same manuals, software, parts, and tools they give their authorized dealers, on the same terms. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the requirement.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use powered wheelchairs, scooters, and wearable robotic walking devices, and the independent repair shops that could fix them. A broken power chair can leave a user homebound for weeks while waiting on a manufacturer-approved repair; the bill lets local shops fix devices on the spot and cuts the cost of repairs that today can run hundreds of dollars.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wheelchair users and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: It creates a copyright-law exception so that bypassing a software lock on a powered wheelchair is legal when the purpose is diagnosis, maintenance, or repair of the device [S2].

It requires manufacturers to sell owners and independent repair providers the documentation, parts, embedded software, firmware, diagnostic tools, and security-lock bypass tools they offer their authorized dealers, at prices no worse than the authorized dealers pay [S2].
It gives the FTC enforcement power and lets state attorneys general sue manufacturers and recover compensation for state residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of powered wheelchairs, scooters, and wearable robotic devices, which lose revenue from service labor, authorized-dealer repair exclusivity, and parts pricing they control today.

drawbacks.text: The bill protects trade secrets and does not require manufacturers to sell parts they no longer make, so some older devices could remain hard to fix [S2].

Manufacturers are shielded from liability for damage or injury caused by a bad independent repair, unless the damage traces back to a design or manufacturing defect — shifting repair risk away from makers and onto repairers [S2].

Device makers argue that opening software locks and distributing diagnostic tools can compromise device security and that untrained repairs of life-supporting mobility equipment carry safety risks — concerns the bill answers by requiring secure data handling but does not eliminate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 1.5 million Americans who use powered wheelchairs or scooters, the benefit is direct and large: faster, cheaper repairs of equipment they depend on daily. The costs fall on manufacturers' service margins and service businesses built around dealer exclusivity. The design is fairly careful — trade secrets, safety carve-outs for manufacturer defects, and liability rules are all spelled out — so the main question is enforcement, not drafting.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, where it has not moved since.

narrative.text: Representative Maxwell Frost introduced the bill on August 26, 2025, joined by Representative Perez as its sole cosponsor [S1][S3].
The Speaker assigned it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, with the Judiciary Committee also getting jurisdiction over the copyright provisions [S4].
No further action — no hearings, markups, or votes — has been recorded since referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, powered mobility device manufacturers: their repair monopoly remains fully intact because the bill has not advanced.

for.name: Rep. Maxwell Frost
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Wheelchair Right to Repair Act and referred it to two committees.

for.name: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members, both Democrats, are on record; no opponent has acted, and no votes have been held.

industries.industry: Powered wheelchair, scooter, and wearable robotic device manufacturers
industries.note: The bill ends their control over who can diagnose and repair their devices and forces parts, manuals, and software tools to be sold at authorized-dealer prices, cutting into service and parts revenue. Device users gain faster, cheaper repairs in return.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and repair providers
industries.note: The bill creates a legal right to access diagnostic software, parts, and manuals, letting these shops compete for repair work now restricted to authorized dealers.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicare/Medicaid durable equipment programs
industries.note: Faster, competitive repairs mean fewer replacements and fewer costly claims for replacement chairs and scooters — public payers and beneficiaries both pay less.

analysis.trajectory: A first-term, single-cosponsor bill referred to two House committees rarely reaches the floor; most die quietly at this stage unless a member moves it, a hearing is scheduled, or it is folded into a larger package. With no action in its first weeks, the realistic outlook is that it stalls unless advocates generate pressure or additional cosponsors.
